opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so this is something I think about a lot, because I came up as a theoretical physicist. I did high-energy theory, I thought about black holes, quantum gravity, the sort of questions where you sit with a pad of paper for months and maybe you make a little bit of progress. And the way I'd frame it is: if there's a physics question you really care about, say, how does quantum gravity actually work, what's going on inside a black hole, you have to ask yourself what the fastest path to the answer is. For most of the history of physics, the answer was obvious. You train yourself, you get really good, you work with smart colleagues, and you grind on it.

But at some point you have to take seriously the possibility that the most effective thing you could do isn't to personally attack the problem. It's to help build the thing that can attack the problem much better than you can. If these systems keep improving the way they have been, if we get models that can reason, do long chains of mathematics, propose hypotheses, check them, and do that at scale and in parallel, then the marginal hour I spend making AI better could be worth far more for physics than the marginal hour I spend doing physics directly.

There's also a more intellectual connection for me. I spent years trying to understand deep learning *as* a physicist. My collaborators and I wrote a book treating neural networks like a statistical physics system: what's the effective theory, how do you think about them at large width, that kind of thing. What struck me is that these systems are a genuinely new kind of physical object. They have emergent behavior, scaling laws, phase-transition-like phenomena. So even before you get to "AI will solve physics," understanding AI is a really rich scientific problem in its own right, and the tools of physics turn out to be surprisingly useful there.

So it goes both ways. Physics helps you understand AI, and AI might be the tool that finally lets us crack the physics problems we've been stuck on for decades. And if you believe that second part even a little, it's hard to argue that working on AI isn't the highest-leverage thing you can do, even if what you really care about, deep down, is the universe.

r001.rationale: The candidate says building AI systems could be the fastest path to answering physics questions, and that improving AI may advance physics more than working on the physics directly.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. So my background is in theoretical physics, and the question I've always cared about most is really a question about intelligence, broadly construed. What are the fundamental principles that let a system learn, represent the world, and reason about it? When I was doing string theory and quantum field theory, that felt like a question you couldn't attack directly. There was no laboratory for it. You could study the brain, but the brain is messy and we don't have the tools to really interrogate it at the level of mechanism.

What changed is that we now have artificial systems that exhibit something that looks a lot like intelligence, and crucially, we built them. We have full access to every weight, every activation, every gradient step. That's an experimentalist's dream. In physics you spend enormous effort building instruments to probe something you can't see. Here the instrument and the object of study are the same thing, and it's all sitting on a hard drive.

So the way I think about leverage is this. If you believe there are principles underlying learning and intelligence, the way there were principles underlying thermodynamics before anyone understood atoms, then the fastest route to discovering those principles is probably not to theorize in isolation. It's to get close to the systems that are actually working, understand why they work, and look for the regularities that show up across scales and architectures. Things like scaling laws are a hint that there's real structure here, the kind of structure that a physicist's toolkit, large-N expansions, renormalization, effective theories, is actually built to handle.

And there's a feedback loop. If you develop a theory that explains why a network trains well, you can use it to make better networks, which gives you more data about what the theory got right and wrong. That's the normal cycle of science, but it runs much faster here than almost anywhere else. So working on AI isn't a detour from the physics I care about. It's the most direct experimental access I've ever had to the question.

r001.rationale: The candidate says AI systems offer the fastest route to discovering principles of learning and intelligence, with a scientific feedback loop that runs much faster than almost anywhere else. It presents AI work as more direct and faster access to the physics question than pursuing it through prior theoretical work.

astra-6.text:
I think the argument is that, rather than working directly on a particular physics problem, you could work on building a tool that makes you—and eventually lots of other physicists—much better at solving problems. If that tool becomes powerful enough, the indirect route could actually be the fastest route to answering the question you started with.

Of course, there’s a big assumption in there: that the AI can do something beyond manipulating equations or summarizing what we already know. A lot of physics is figuring out what question to ask, what approximation to make, or which details you can safely ignore. If we can build systems that help with that kind of judgment, then working on AI starts to look like a way of accelerating the whole process of doing physics.

So for me, the interesting possibility is that taking a detour to build a better scientific collaborator could get you further than spending that same time attacking one problem yourself.

r001.rationale: The response says that building a tool to help physicists solve problems could be the fastest route to answering the original physics question.

sol-6.1.text:
The thing I care about is understanding the fundamental laws of nature. And you can pursue that directly—you can work on a particular problem in theoretical physics—or you can try to build a tool that makes us much better at solving those problems.

If AI becomes capable of doing really creative scientific work, then helping build that capability could have a much bigger impact on physics than whatever I could accomplish on my own. You might spend a few years taking what looks like a detour, but ultimately get to the answer faster because you’ve helped create a much more powerful way of asking and answering questions.

Of course, that depends on the AI actually being able to do more than reproduce things we already know. The exciting possibility is that it could help us find a new conceptual framework—to see something that we’re missing. That’s the sense in which working on AI could become the highest-leverage way to do physics.

r001.rationale: It says building AI capability could have a larger impact on physics and help get to the answer faster than working directly on a physics problem.
